summary:
Cosmos 1 is a public-facing astronomy explorer for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, built by Adharv Kodali and Reyansh Vanga. Its goal is to help people explore how the sky changes by comparing SPHEREx observations over time.

Visitors can enter sky coordinates in decimal degrees or sexagesimal format, or start with one of the five challenge targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. The app searches SPHEREx archive records through IRSA, lets users select dated observations in the same wavelength band, and plays the loaded images as a timeline. Playback speed is adjustable.

The prototype also includes image comparison and change-analysis tools, a research notebook and FITS exports, science learning tools, a sky catalog, mission history, and SkyShift, an astronomy assistant. Its AR Museum offers WebXR on compatible devices and a camera-based fallback where available.

The app distinguishes real archive images from its synthetic training sequence. Archive coverage varies by target, and raw images may need registration and specialist checks before apparent changes can be treated as real discoveries.
details:
Cosmos 1 is a public-facing tool for exploring how sky images change over time. It supports NASA’s SPHEREx challenge by letting people search a sky patch by Right Ascension and declination, then compare available observations as a short, playable sequence.

Visitors can enter coordinates in decimal degrees or sexagesimal format, or start with the challenge targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. The app queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), lists available observations, and lets users select dates from the same wavelength band. It loads usable FITS cutouts in date order so users can play, pause, scrub, slow down, blink between images, and compare them.

The workbench includes image-difference candidate detection, source tracking, brightness and spectral tools, observation notes, reports, and FITS exports. SkyShift, the astronomy assistant, explains mission science and the measurements available to the app. The AR Museum offers an interactive sky catalog and mission history, with WebXR on compatible devices and a camera-based fallback where supported.

The project’s intended impact is to make time-domain astronomy easier to try for students, educators, and the public. Turning archive visits into a visual sequence can help people notice possible motion or brightness changes and decide what to investigate next. Coordinate presets for the five challenge objects provide a starting point for testing and exploration.

The prototype was built with TypeScript, React, Next.js, and Three.js, with a Cloudflare Worker handling archive and AI requests. It uses public SPHEREx data through NASA/IPAC IRSA and public constellation catalog data. SkyShift uses a Groq-hosted language model. The app runs in a web browser; a camera-capable phone is optional for the AR experience.

A key design choice was to separate real archive observations from synthetic training images. The app also explains that raw images may need alignment, wavelength matching, and quality checks before apparent changes can be interpreted. Candidate detections are leads for review, not confirmed discoveries. The team considered coordinate formats, target proper motion, archive coverage, image-size mismatches, mobile use, keyboard navigation, reduced motion, and color accessibility.
